title: Shankara sings to Govinda
hookLine: the great teacher of knowing hears an old scholar cramming grammar, and answers him with a song to Govinda
carry: jnana and bhakti, knowing and loving, meet
tomorrow: Fear not: the guru shows the way

cards: Kashi again. Shankara is walking by when he hears an old man drilling himself on Sanskrit grammar, the same rule over and over, dukrin karane, dukrin karane, as if his life depended on it.
The man is near the end of his life, and still memorizing. And Shankara, the great teacher of knowing, doesn't hand him an argument. Tradition says he sings to him.
The song begins: Bhaja Govindam. Worship Govinda.

teach.b: The first verse, in paraphrase: worship Govinda, worship Govinda, worship Govinda, foolish mind. When your time comes, the grammar rule won't save you.
That's Govinda from our kirtan four days ago, Krishna's cowherd name, on the lips of the philosopher of knowing. The Vivekachudamani, also credited to Shankara, shows why that's no contradiction.

teach.h: DISCERNMENT, LETTING GO, SIX TREASURES, LONGING.
teach.b: It names four things a seeker needs: viveka, discernment between the lasting and the passing; vairagya, letting go of the hunger for enjoyments; six treasures, among them calm, restraint, endurance and faith; and the longing to be free.
If letting go and longing are weak, it says, the rest are like mirages in a desert.
Then the surprise, in paraphrase: among all the means to freedom, bhakti, devotion, is the greatest.
And bhakti, the text says, is the seeking of one's own true nature.
Hindus often speak of jnana and bhakti, knowing and loving, as two paths. Here they meet. Shankara's tradition credits him with both the hard arguments and the hymns.
The old scholar's mistake wasn't studying. It was mistaking the rule for the goal.
To love the truth of who you are enough to keep looking for it: on this reading, that's bhakti, and it's what the singing and the book were both for.

how: In Advaita teaching, the four qualifications, discernment, dispassion, the six treasures and the longing for freedom, are taught as preparation for the main texts, and students work on them as daily disciplines.

o: a set of rules for living in a monastery
a cold path of logic that leaves no room for love
knowing that frees, built on discernment and longing

games.q: what the seeker brings — tap the pairs.
p: letting go of the hunger for enjoyment
Shankara's song to a grammar-cramming scholar

s: a book about knowing has no room for devotion
the Vivekachudamani calls bhakti the greatest of the means to freedom, and defines it as seeking one's own true nature.
without dispassion and longing, the text says calm and the rest are like mirages
if those two are weak, the others are like water in a desert that isn't there.
Shankara answered the old scholar with an argument
tradition says he sang: worship Govinda, foolish mind; the grammar rule won't save you.

games.q: you're writing a book on the path of knowing. you've listed discernment, letting go, calm and longing. which do you call the greatest means to freedom?
games.why: the Vivekachudamani names bhakti, and defines it as the seeking of one's own true nature.

practice: Let the eyes close and sort your day so far into two piles: things that were passing, a mood, a headline, a craving, a small worry, and anything that seemed to stay.
Don't argue about which pile something goes in; just practice the sorting, which is viveka in a small way.
If you pray, say Govinda's name once, softly, as Shankara sang it to the old scholar; if not, hold the longing to know what lasts.

wordCard.voice: Jnana. Knowing that frees. In the Vivekachudamani it rests on discernment, letting go and longing, and the text calls the seeking of your own nature bhakti.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: viveka, discernment, telling the lasting from the passing. The first word of the book's title.

carryVoice: Your line: jnana and bhakti, knowing and loving, meet. Even the road of knowing runs on love. That's day nine hundred ninety-four.
